Draft Product Information
Date: 1 June 2022
Page 1 of 5
 STATUS OF THIS DOCUMENT
Kelvaparib is an investigational product and holds no marketing authorisation in any
country. This document is the company core data sheet maintained during clinical
development. It states the information the sponsor proposes for the product information
at the time of a marketing application, and is the reference against which proposed
labelling changes are assessed. Expectedness for expedited reporting is determined
against the reference safety information, Section 7 of the Investigator's Brochure (filed as
reference-safety-information-kelvaparib), the sole governing document for listedness.

1. NAME OF THE MEDICINAL PRODUCT
Kelvaparib 150 mg film-coated tablets.

2. QUALITATIVE AND QUANTITATIVE COMPOSITION
Each film-coated tablet contains 150 mg of kelvaparib. The recommended dose is
administered as two tablets twice daily.

3. PHARMACEUTICAL FORM
Film-coated tablet for oral administration.

4. CLINICAL PARTICULARS
4.1 Therapeutic indications
Kelvaparib is proposed as maintenance monotherapy for adults with recurrent high-grade
serous ovarian carcinoma after prior platinum-based chemotherapy. The proposed
indication is supported by study KLV-7701, a randomised, placebo-controlled study of
kelvaparib as maintenance therapy.

4.2 Posology and method of administration
The recommended dose is 300 mg orally twice daily on a continuous schedule. Treatment
should continue until disease progression, unacceptable toxicity or withdrawal of
consent. Tablets should be swallowed whole and may be taken with or without food.

Dose modification. For a grade 3 or higher haematological adverse reaction, treatment
should be withheld until recovery to grade 1 or baseline and resumed at 225 mg twice
daily. A second reduction to 150 mg twice daily is permitted. Treatment should be
discontinued if a grade 3 or higher reaction recurs at the lowest dose, or where
haematological recovery has not occurred within 28 days.

Older subjects. No dose adjustment by age is proposed. Exposure did not differ
materially with age in the population pharmacokinetic analysis. Dose reduction and
discontinuation for an adverse reaction were more frequent in subjects aged 75 years and



Indication: High-grade serous ovarian carcinoma
Product: Kelvaparib (KLV-3308)
Draft Product Information
Date: 1 June 2022
Page 2 of 5
 above than in younger subjects, and closer haematological monitoring is advised in that
group.

Hepatic and renal impairment. No dose recommendation can be made in severe hepatic or
severe renal impairment, because subjects with severe impairment were excluded from the
clinical programme. No dose adjustment is proposed for mild or moderate impairment.

4.3 Contraindications
Hypersensitivity to kelvaparib or to any of the excipients. Breast-feeding.

4.4 Special warnings and precautions for use
Myelosuppression
Myelosuppression is an important identified risk and is the most frequent reason for
dose modification. In study KLV-7701 anaemia was reported in 202 of 418 subjects (48.3
per cent), thrombocytopenia in 101 subjects (24.2 per cent), neutropenia in 83 subjects
(19.9 per cent) and leukopenia in 44 subjects (10.5 per cent).

Treatment should not begin until haematological recovery from prior chemotherapy is
complete. Full blood count should be measured before the first dose, weekly for the
first month and monthly thereafter. Treatment should be withheld for a
grade 3 or higher cytopenia and resumed at a reduced dose on recovery. Where a cytopenia
has not recovered within 28 days, haematological consultation and bone marrow
examination should be considered.

Myelodysplastic syndrome and acute myeloid leukaemia
Myelodysplastic syndrome and acute myeloid leukaemia are an important identified risk
and have been observed in the clinical programme, in 9 subjects (1.4 per cent) in study
KLV-7701. Both have a latency substantially longer than the duration of exposure in the
completed studies, so the cumulative incidence is expected to rise with further follow-
up and should not be read as final.

A cytopenia that persists beyond 28 days, or a blood count abnormality that is
disproportionate to recent exposure, should prompt bone marrow examination and
cytogenetic analysis rather than continued dose modification. Where myelodysplastic
syndrome or acute myeloid leukaemia is confirmed, treatment should be discontinued
permanently and the subject referred for haematological management. Long-term follow-up
for these events continues for five years after the last dose irrespective of the reason
for discontinuation.

Style and Terminology Guide
Edition 3, effective 1 March 2021
Page 1 of 4
 1. PURPOSE AND SCOPE
This guide states the house conventions that apply to every clinical document prepared
for the kelvaparib programme, including clinical study reports and their appendices,
protocols and amendments, statistical analysis plans, synopses and periodic safety
reports. It governs expression, terminology and presentation. It does not govern
document architecture, which follows ICH E3 for clinical study reports and the
applicable ICH guideline for other document types.

Where this guide and an ICH guideline both address a point, the guideline prevails and
this guide is read as supplementing it. Where a departure from this guide is deliberate,
the reason is recorded in the document review record.

2. DOCUMENT IDENTIFICATION AND VERSION CONTROL
• Every page carries the product name with its development code, the document type and
  the document date, in that order.

• Every page carries a page number in the form "Page n of N".

• The indication is stated on every page of documents that span more than one study.

3. COMPOUND, ARM AND TREATMENT NAMING
• The compound is named "kelvaparib" in body text. The development code KLV-3308 is
  used at first mention in a document, in page footers and on title pages, and is not
  repeated in body text thereafter.

• In a randomised study, arm labels state the agent and the dose, as in "Kelvaparib
  300 mg". The comparator is named as it appears in the protocol, and is not
  abbreviated.

• In a dose-escalation study, cohorts are labelled by dose alone, as in "300 mg",
  because the agent is common to every cohort.

• Arm and cohort labels are identical in every table, figure, listing and narrative
  within a document set. A label is not shortened to fit a column.

4. TERMINOLOGY
• Adverse event terminology follows the coding dictionary in force. Verbatim terms are
  not used in narrative text where a coded preferred term exists.

• "Subject" is used throughout, not "patient", in clinical study reports and their
  appendices. "Patient" is permitted in documents written for a non-technical
  readership.

Product: Kelvaparib (KLV-3308)

• British spelling is used, except within a coded term, a proper noun or a quotation,
  where the source spelling is preserved.

5. UNITS, NUMBERS AND PERCENTAGES
• Units follow the International System of Units. A space separates the value from the
  unit, as in "300 mg".

• Percentages are written as "per cent" in body text. The symbol is reserved for table
  column headers and for parenthetical values within a table cell.

• Percentages are reported to one decimal place. A percentage is suppressed where the
  denominator is fewer than five, and the denominator is stated wherever a percentage
  appears.

• Time is reported in the unit specified by the analysis plan, and the same unit is
  used for the same quantity throughout a document.

• Every document contains a list of abbreviations, placed before the first numbered

• An abbreviation is expanded at first use in body text and thereafter used alone.

• An abbreviation is not introduced in a table or figure unless it also appears in the

 • Missing values are represented by an empty field.
 • Subject identifiers take the form STUDYID-nnnn and are unique across the programme.
 • Centre identifiers are recorded as four-digit codes; investigator names are not held in the

Primary endpoint

Progression-free survival, defined as the time from the first dose of study
treatment to the first documented disease progression by investigator
assessment or death from any cause, whichever occurs first.

Key secondary endpoints

Duration of response, overall survival and the incidence and severity of
treatment-emergent adverse events.

Statistical methods

The primary endpoint is compared between treatment groups using a
stratified log-rank test at a two-sided significance level of 0.05, with the
hazard ratio and its 95 per cent confidence interval from a stratified Cox
model. Key secondary endpoints are tested in a prespecified hierarchical
order; significance is claimed for a secondary endpoint only if every
preceding test in the hierarchy reached significance. Approximately 388
events provide 90 per cent power to detect a hazard ratio of 0.71.

1 INTRODUCTION
1.1 Background to the disease
High-grade serous ovarian carcinoma is the indication under study in this protocol. The
population enrolled here has disease that has progressed after, or is unsuitable for, the therapy
ordinarily offered first, and the outcomes reported for that population remain poor. Treatment at
this stage is given with the intention of controlling disease, delaying deterioration and preserving
function, and the size of that benefit with existing options is modest. There is therefore a
recognised need for agents that act by a mechanism not already exploited in earlier lines.
The natural history of the disease and the outcomes achieved with current management were
reviewed when this protocol was written. That review informed the choice of comparator, the
endpoints, the assessment schedule and the assumptions underlying the sample size in Section
8.1.
The population studied in this protocol has recurrent ovarian carcinoma after prior
platinum-based therapy, platinum-sensitive or platinum-resistant. Disease at this point in the
pathway behaves differently from disease at presentation: it has already been selected by
exposure to prior therapy, and the mechanisms that allowed it to persist through that therapy are
the mechanisms that determine what happens next. That selection is why response rates fall
and why the duration of any response shortens with each successive line.
The clinical course is dominated by the accumulation of disease-related morbidity alongside the
cumulative toxicity of previous treatment. Subjects entering a study at this stage typically carry a
burden of unresolved effects from earlier lines, which constrains what can safely be given and
which is the reason the eligibility criteria in Section 4 require recovery from prior toxicity before a
subject may start study treatment.

Statistical methods

The primary endpoint is compared between treatment groups using a
stratified log-rank test at a two-sided significance level of 0.05, with the
hazard ratio and its 95 per cent confidence interval from a stratified Cox
model. Key secondary endpoints are tested in a prespecified hierarchical

events provide 90 per cent power to detect a hazard ratio of 0.71.

The overall response rate was Kelvaparib 300 mg 250 of 405 subjects
(61.7 per cent, 95 per cent CI (56.8, 66.5)); Placebo 79 of 199 subjects
(39.7 per cent, 95 per cent CI (32.8, 46.9)). Complete response was
reported in 64 subjects (10.6 per cent) overall. Median progression-free

recurrent ovarian carcinoma (stratified hazard ratio 0.64, 95 per cent CI

met. The objective response rate (54.5 per cent) was also significantly

5.6.1 Dosing schedule
Kelvaparib is supplied as film-coated tablets and administered orally twice daily on a continuous
schedule. The schedule administers the assigned dose with weekly blood counts in weeks 1 to
4, the assigned dose with monthly blood counts in week 5 onwards.
5.6.2 Myelosuppression prophylaxis and monitoring
All subjects receive full blood count before treatment, weekly for the first month and monthly
thereafter, with dose interruption for grade 3 or higher cytopenia and prompt haematology
referral for any cytopenia persisting beyond four weeks. Subjects at high risk, defined as a
haemoglobin below 110 g/L at baseline, three or more prior lines of platinum-based therapy, or
prior pelvic radiotherapy, additionally receive intravenous hydration and laboratory monitoring
before the first dose and at 4, 8, 12 and 24 hours after it.
5.6.3 Modification for myelosuppression
For grade 4 haematological toxicity or grade 3 or higher non-haematological toxicity considered
related to study treatment, dosing is withheld until recovery to grade 1 or baseline and resumed
at the next lower dose level. No more than two dose reductions are permitted. For laboratory
myelosuppression, dosing is withheld with daily monitoring; treatment resumes at the same dose
with intensified prophylaxis if laboratory-only, and at the next lower dose level if clinical
myelosuppression occurred.

inducers are prohibited. Where a moderate inhibitor cannot be avoided the dose is reduced by at

concurred.

1. SAFETY SPECIFICATION
Important identified risks are Myelosuppression, myelodysplastic syndrome or acute myeloid
leukaemia, and pneumonitis. Important potential risks are second primary malignancy and
effects on fertility. Missing information includes use in severe hepatic impairment, use in
pregnancy and long-term safety beyond three years of exposure.

2. PHARMACOVIGILANCE PLAN
Routine pharmacovigilance applies to all identified and potential risks. Additional activities
comprise a dedicated hepatic impairment study and a long-term follow-up registry.

3. RISK MINIMISATION MEASURES
Routine measures comprise the product information, including a full blood count before the first
dose, weekly for the first month and monthly thereafter, and the rule to withhold treatment for a
grade 3 or higher cytopenia and resume at a reduced dose (section 4.4 of the product
information). Additional measures comprise a prescriber guide and a patient card describing the
monitoring schedule.

4. SUMMARY
The plan is proportionate to the identified risks and relies principally on the monitoring and
dose-modification measures validated during clinical development.

Appendix 3 ADVERSE EVENT DEFINITIONS AND REPORTING
An adverse event is any untoward medical occurrence in a subject administered a medicinal
product, whether or not related to that product. A serious adverse event is one that results in
death, is life-threatening, requires or prolongs hospitalisation, results in persistent or significant
disability or incapacity, is a congenital anomaly or birth defect, or is an important medical event
that may jeopardise the subject or require intervention to prevent one of the preceding
outcomes.
Adverse events are collected from the signing of consent to the end of study participation, and
serious adverse events considered related to study treatment are collected without time limit.
Severity is graded using the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events. Causality is
assessed by the investigator as related or not related, and an assessment of not related requires
an alternative explanation to be recorded.
Serious adverse events are reported to the sponsor within 24 hours of the site becoming aware.
The sponsor assesses expectedness against the reference safety information in the investigator
brochure and submits expedited reports to the authorities, ethics committees and investigators
within the timelines required in each territory: 7 calendar days for a fatal or life-threatening
suspected unexpected serious adverse reaction and 15 calendar days otherwise.

A woman is of childbearing potential unless she is postmenopausal, defined as 12 months of

7.2 Safety assessments
Safety assessment comprises adverse event enquiry, physical examination, vital signs,
performance status, 12-lead electrocardiogram and the laboratory panels in Table 8 (Appendix
2). Laboratory results are graded using the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events.
Safety assessment is deliberately more frequent early in treatment, when the events of special
interest are most likely to occur, and is reduced once a subject has passed the period of greatest
risk without incident. The schedule in Table 5 reflects that.
Laboratory results are graded using the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events. A
laboratory abnormality is recorded as an adverse event where it is clinically significant, where it
requires intervention, or where it leads to a change in study treatment; otherwise it is captured
as laboratory data alone. This convention is applied consistently, because inconsistency
between sites in what is recorded as an event is a common source of apparent difference in
safety profile.
Vital signs are measured after the subject has been at rest for at least five minutes and, where a
post-dose measurement is required, at the interval specified for the route of administration.
Electrocardiograms are recorded in triplicate at screening and as single tracings thereafter
unless an abnormality requires repetition.
All samples are analysed at the central laboratory. Local results may be used for immediate clinical decisions and are recorded
where they lead to a dose change.

Haematology. The expected haematological effect of this product is the reason for the frequency
of this panel early in treatment. A fall that is progressive across consecutive measurements is
treated differently from a single low value, and the dose modification rules in Table 4 are applied
to the confirmed value.
Clinical chemistry. Hepatic and renal parameters are the ones that most often lead to a change
in study treatment. A rise in transaminase together with a rise in bilirubin is handled under
Appendix 10 rather than under the general rules, because the combination has a specific
meaning.
Coagulation. Assessed at the intervals in Table 5 and whenever a bleeding event occurs.
Results are interpreted alongside the platelet count rather than in isolation.
Urinalysis. A screening test. An abnormal result is followed by microscopy and, where it persists,
by quantification of proteinuria.

Statistical methods

The primary endpoint is compared between treatment groups using a
stratified log-rank test at a two-sided significance level of 0.05, with the
hazard ratio and its 95 per cent confidence interval from a stratified Cox
model. Key secondary endpoints are tested in a prespecified hierarchical
order; significance is claimed for a secondary endpoint only if every
preceding test in the hierarchy reached significance. Approximately 388
events provide 90 per cent power to detect a hazard ratio of 0.71.

Summary - efficacy

The overall response rate was Kelvaparib 300 mg 250 of 405 subjects
(61.7 per cent, 95 per cent CI (56.8, 66.5)); Placebo 79 of 199 subjects
(39.7 per cent, 95 per cent CI (32.8, 46.9)). Complete response was
reported in 64 subjects (10.6 per cent) overall. Median progression-free
survival 8.2 months.

Summary - safety

Grade 3 or higher events in 298 subjects (47.5 per cent), serious events in
159 (25.4 per cent). Nausea was the most frequent event (393 subjects,
62.7 per cent). Myelodysplastic syndrome or acute myeloid leukaemia, an
event of special interest, occurred in 9 subjects (1.4 per cent). 96
discontinued because of an adverse event; 139 deaths were reported.

Conclusion

Kelvaparib prolonged progression-free survival compared with placebo in
recurrent ovarian carcinoma (stratified hazard ratio 0.64, 95 per cent CI
0.50 to 0.81; stratified log-rank p = 0.0002), and the primary endpoint was
met. The objective response rate (54.5 per cent) was also significantly
higher with kelvaparib (p < 0.0001); overall survival did not differ (p =
0.8651).

Treatment-emergent adverse events graded by CTCAE version 5.0,

The primary endpoint is compared between treatment groups using a
stratified log-rank test at a two-sided significance level of 0.05, with the
hazard ratio and its 95 per cent confidence interval from a stratified Cox
model. Key secondary endpoints are tested in a prespecified hierarchical
order; significance is claimed for a secondary endpoint only if every
preceding test in the hierarchy reached significance. Approximately 388
events provide 90 per cent power to detect a hazard ratio of 0.71.

(57.2 per cent, 95 per cent CI (52.1, 62.2)); Placebo 69 of 188 subjects

reported in 54 subjects (9.5 per cent) overall. Median progression-free
survival 8.2 months.

Methodology

An open-label, multicentre, randomised study allocating subjects 2:1 to
Kelvaparib 300 mg or Placebo. Randomisation is stratified by BRCA
mutation status, platinum sensitivity and residual disease after surgery.
Approximately 627 subjects.

Number of subjects

627 subjects were randomised and received at least one dose of study
treatment (418 Kelvaparib 300 mg, 209 Placebo).

Diagnosis and main criteria for
inclusion

Adults with histologically or cytologically confirmed recurrent ovarian
carcinoma after prior platinum-based therapy, platinum-sensitive or
platinum-resistant, measurable disease assessable by RECIST version
1.1, ECOG performance status 0 or 1, adequate organ function.

Test product, dose and mode
of administration

Kelvaparib, film-coated tablets, administered orally twice daily on a
continuous schedule, with weekly blood counts for the first month and
monthly thereafter.

Duration of treatment

Until disease progression, unacceptable toxicity or withdrawal of consent.
Median duration 119 days.

Criteria for evaluation - efficacy Best overall response by RECIST version 1.1, and duration of response,
progression-free survival, overall survival.
Criteria for evaluation - safety

Treatment-emergent adverse events graded by CTCAE version 5.0,
laboratory parameters and vital signs.

Page 2 of 78

 Product: Kelvaparib (KLV-3308)
Clinical Study Report: KLV-7701
Date: 28 November 2022
Statistical methods

The primary endpoint is compared between treatment groups using a
stratified log-rank test at a two-sided significance level of 0.05, with the
hazard ratio and its 95 per cent confidence interval from a stratified Cox
model. Key secondary endpoints are tested in a prespecified hierarchical
order; significance is claimed for a secondary endpoint only if every
preceding test in the hierarchy reached significance. Approximately 388
events provide 90 per cent power to detect a hazard ratio of 0.71.

Summary - efficacy

The overall response rate was Kelvaparib 300 mg 250 of 405 subjects
(61.7 per cent, 95 per cent CI (56.8, 66.5)); Placebo 79 of 199 subjects
(39.7 per cent, 95 per cent CI (32.8, 46.9)). Complete response was
reported in 64 subjects (10.6 per cent) overall. Median progression-free
survival 8.2 months.

Summary - safety

Grade 3 or higher events in 298 subjects (47.5 per cent), serious events in
159 (25.4 per cent). Nausea was the most frequent event (393 subjects,
62.7 per cent). Myelodysplastic syndrome or acute myeloid leukaemia, an
event of special interest, occurred in 9 subjects (1.4 per cent). 96
discontinued because of an adverse event; 139 deaths were reported.

Conclusion

Kelvaparib prolonged progression-free survival compared with placebo in
recurrent ovarian carcinoma (stratified hazard ratio 0.64, 95 per cent CI
0.50 to 0.81; stratified log-rank p = 0.0002), and the primary endpoint was
met. The objective response rate (54.5 per cent) was also significantly
higher with kelvaparib (p < 0.0001); overall survival did not differ (p =
0.8651).

1.2 Background to the investigational product
Kelvaparib (KLV-3308) is an oral PARP1-selective inhibitor. Its mechanism is distinct from the
agents used earlier in the treatment pathway, which provides the rationale for studying it in a
population that has already been exposed to those agents.
The product is presented as film-coated tablets and is administered orally twice daily on a
continuous schedule . Details of preparation, storage and handling are given in Section 5.2 and
in the pharmacy manual.
Exposure after administration has been characterised in the studies described in the investigator
brochure. The dose selected for this study, and the dose levels available for reduction in an
individual subject, follow from that characterisation together with the relationship between
exposure and toxicity; the reasoning is set out in Section 3.3.
The principal identified risk associated with this mechanism is myelodysplastic syndrome or
acute myeloid leukaemia. It is predictable in its timing, it is detectable by the monitoring in Table
5 before it becomes clinically significant in most subjects, and it is manageable by the dose
modification in Table 4 and the measures in Appendix 5. Those three facts together are what
make it acceptable to study the product in this population.
High-grade serous ovarian carcinoma carries a poor long-term prognosis. Women with
platinum-resistant disease, residual disease after surgery, or homologous recombination
proficient tumours have the shortest progression-free survival.
Kelvaparib (KLV-3308) is an oral PARP1-selective inhibitor. By selectively inhibiting and trapping
poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase 1 on damaged DNA it prevents single-strand break repair, so that
replication forks collapse into double-strand breaks that tumours deficient in homologous
recombination cannot repair. Because the effect is rapid and extensive, myelosuppression is a

5.6.2 Myelosuppression prophylaxis and monitoring
All subjects receive full blood count before treatment, weekly for the first month and monthly
thereafter, with dose interruption for grade 3 or higher cytopenia and prompt haematology

before the first dose and at 4, 8, 12 and 24 hours after it.

7.2 Safety assessments
Safety assessment comprises adverse event enquiry, physical examination, vital signs,
performance status, 12-lead electrocardiogram and the laboratory panels in Table 8 (Appendix
2). Laboratory results are graded using the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events.
Safety assessment is deliberately more frequent early in treatment, when the events of special
interest are most likely to occur, and is reduced once a subject has passed the period of greatest
risk without incident. The schedule in Table 5 reflects that.
Laboratory results are graded using the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events. A
laboratory abnormality is recorded as an adverse event where it is clinically significant, where it
requires intervention, or where it leads to a change in study treatment; otherwise it is captured
as laboratory data alone. This convention is applied consistently, because inconsistency
between sites in what is recorded as an event is a common source of apparent difference in
safety profile.
Vital signs are measured after the subject has been at rest for at least five minutes and, where a
post-dose measurement is required, at the interval specified for the route of administration.
Electrocardiograms are recorded in triplicate at screening and as single tracings thereafter
unless an abnormality requires repetition.
All samples are analysed at the central laboratory. Local results may be used for immediate clinical decisions and are recorded
where they lead to a dose change.

Haematology. The expected haematological effect of this product is the reason for the frequency
of this panel early in treatment. A fall that is progressive across consecutive measurements is
treated differently from a single low value, and the dose modification rules in Table 4 are applied
to the confirmed value.
Clinical chemistry. Hepatic and renal parameters are the ones that most often lead to a change
in study treatment. A rise in transaminase together with a rise in bilirubin is handled under
Appendix 10 rather than under the general rules, because the combination has a specific
meaning.
Coagulation. Assessed at the intervals in Table 5 and whenever a bleeding event occurs.
Results are interpreted alongside the platelet count rather than in isolation.
Urinalysis. A screening test. An abnormal result is followed by microscopy and, where it persists,
by quantification of proteinuria.

This guide states the house conventions that apply to every clinical document prepared

2. DOCUMENT IDENTIFICATION AND VERSION CONTROL

13 DISCUSSION AND OVERALL CONCLUSIONS

Study KLV-7701 evaluated kelvaparib in recurrent ovarian carcinoma after prior platinum-based therapy, platinum-sensitive or
platinum-resistant. Kelvaparib prolonged progression-free survival compared with placebo in recurrent ovarian carcinoma after prior
platinum-based therapy, platinum-sensitive or platinum-resistant (stratified hazard ratio 0.64, 95 per cent CI 0.50 to 0.81; stratified
log-rank p = 0.0002), and the primary endpoint was met. The objective response rate (54.5 per cent) was also significantly higher with
kelvaparib (Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel p < 0.0001); overall survival, the next endpoint in the testing hierarchy, did not differ (stratified
log-rank p = 0.8651), and findings below that point are descriptive. The safety profile was dominated by anaemia and myelosuppression,
both on-target consequences of the mechanism of action. Myelodysplastic syndrome or acute myeloid leukaemia occurred in 1.4 per cent
of subjects (Section 12.2.6). Limitations should be borne in mind. The study was open-label, which may influence investigator
assessment of response and reporting of subjective adverse events. Follow-up was ongoing at the data cut-off and time-to-event
estimates are therefore immature. Taken together, the results of study KLV-7701 support the continued development of kelvaparib at 300
mg, with weekly blood counts for the first month and monthly thereafter, in high-grade serous ovarian carcinoma.

The population enrolled was consistent with the intended population and with the eligibility criteria. Exposure was sufficient to
characterise both the efficacy and the safety of the regimen. The primary analysis was performed as planned; the sensitivity analyses the
statistical analysis plan lists are not reported here.

The population enrolled was the population the protocol described. Median age, performance status and prior therapy were consistent
with the eligibility criteria, and there is no indication that the study enrolled a population easier to treat than the one intended.

Exposure was adequate. The median relative dose intensity indicates that the regimen as written could be delivered, and the pattern of
reduction and interruption was consistent with the toxicities anticipated for oral PARP1-selective inhibitor.

The efficacy result should be read together with its confidence interval and with the maturity of the follow-up. Because the study was
randomised, the comparison is internally controlled and the estimate does not depend on an external assumption about how this
population would otherwise have fared.

The safety profile was consistent with the mechanism and with the earlier clinical experience. The events reported most often, and those
most often reaching grade 3 or higher, were those for which the protocol required specific monitoring, which indicates that the monitoring
was directed at the right things.

96 subjects (15.3 per cent) discontinued study treatment because of an adverse event. That figure, rather than the overall incidence of

modification.

Deaths were reviewed individually. Those attributed to an adverse event are described in the narratives; the remainder are recorded as

1.3 Non-clinical experience

Non-clinical pharmacology established activity at exposures achievable in the clinic and
characterised the relationship between exposure and effect. Safety pharmacology found no
effect on central nervous, respiratory or cardiovascular function at exposures within the intended
clinical range. Repeat-dose toxicology in two species identified the target organs described in
the investigator brochure; the findings were monitorable, and reversible on withdrawal at the
exposures tested. Genotoxicity assays were negative. The full non-clinical package, including
the derivation of the starting dose, is in the investigator brochure.

Primary pharmacology established activity in the relevant models at exposures that are
achievable in the clinic, and characterised the relationship between exposure and effect. That
relationship was used to define the exposure the clinical dose is intended to achieve.

Secondary pharmacology screening against a panel of receptors, ion channels, transporters and
enzymes did not identify off-target activity at concentrations within the intended clinical range

8. Adequate bone marrow function: absolute neutrophil count at or above 1.0 x 10^9/L, platelets
at or above 100 x 10^9/L and haemoglobin at or above 80 g/L, without transfusion or growth
factor support in the 7 days before screening. Rationale. The thresholds are set so that a subject
has the reserve to tolerate the expected haematological effect. They are deliberately not so strict
as to exclude subjects whose counts reflect disease rather than frailty.

9. Adequate hepatic function: total bilirubin at or below 1.5 times the upper limit of normal, and
alanine and aspartate aminotransferase at or below 3 times the upper limit of normal, or 5 times
in the presence of hepatic involvement by the underlying disease. Rationale. Hepatic impairment
alters exposure and reduces the margin before hepatotoxicity becomes clinically significant. The
allowance for disease involvement of the liver reflects that a raised transaminase in that setting
has a different meaning.

10. Adequate renal function: creatinine clearance at or above 50 mL/min estimated by the
Cockcroft-Gault formula. Rationale. The threshold reflects the contribution of renal elimination to
clearance and the exposure that would result at lower function. Subjects below it would receive
an exposure the safety data do not cover.

11. Recovery from the acute toxic effects of prior therapy to grade 1 or baseline, other than
alopecia and stable peripheral neuropathy. Rationale. Entering a study before recovery from
prior therapy makes it impossible to attribute a subsequent event, and compounds toxicity in a
way that neither the eligibility criteria nor the dose modification rules were designed to handle.

12. Women of childbearing potential must have a negative serum pregnancy test at screening
and agree to use a highly effective method of contraception for the period defined in Appendix 4.
Rationale. The reproductive toxicity package is incomplete, so the requirement is absolute and is
verified at screening and repeated during treatment as scheduled in Table 5.

13. Men must agree to use a barrier method and to refrain from donating sperm for the period
defined in Appendix 4. Rationale. The requirement for men reflects the interval over which the
product and its metabolites may be present in seminal fluid, with a margin.

14. Willing and able to comply with the schedule of assessments, the study restrictions and the
requirements of long-term follow-up. Rationale. A study of this intensity depends on attendance.
This criterion is about the practicability of participation for the subject, not about their motivation,
and it is assessed with them rather than about them.

Guidance on the management of the events of special interest. Each event in this appendix is

under the rule in Section 5.6.3, in addition to the management below.

Myelodysplastic syndrome or acute myeloid leukaemia

Presentation. Myelodysplastic syndrome or acute myeloid leukaemia associated with Kelvaparib
is most likely to occur during the period of most intensive monitoring in Table 5. Its early
manifestations may be non-specific, which is why the monitoring is scheduled rather than
prompted by symptoms.

Monitoring. The assessments in Table 5 are performed at the scheduled times irrespective of
whether the subject reports symptoms. Any assessment suggesting the event is repeated within
24 to 72 hours, and the subject is reviewed by a clinician before the next dose.

Management at grade 1. Continue study treatment. Increase the frequency of the relevant
assessment to at least weekly until the abnormality resolves or is stable, and record the event.

Management at grade 2. Withhold study treatment. Investigate for alternative causes, including
concomitant medication and the underlying disease. Treat according to local practice and the
guidance in the investigator brochure. Resume at the same dose only if the event resolves to
grade 1 or baseline within 14 days; otherwise resume at one dose level lower.

122: 1.2 Background to the investigational product
123: 
124: Kelvaparib (KLV-3308) is an oral PARP1-selective inhibitor. Its mechanism is distinct from the
125: agents used earlier in the treatment pathway, which provides the rationale for studying it in a
126: population that has already been exposed to those agents.
127: 
128: The product is presented as film-coated tablets and is administered orally twice daily on a
129: continuous schedule . Details of preparation, storage and handling are given in Section 5.2 and
130: in the pharmacy manual.
131: 
132: Exposure after administration has been characterised in the studies described in the investigator
133: brochure. The dose selected for this study, and the dose levels available for reduction in an
134: individual subject, follow from that characterisation together with the relationship between
135: exposure and toxicity; the reasoning is set out in Section 3.3.
136: 
137: The principal identified risk associated with this mechanism is myelodysplastic syndrome or
138: acute myeloid leukaemia. It is predictable in its timing, it is detectable by the monitoring in Table
139: 5 before it becomes clinically significant in most subjects, and it is manageable by the dose
140: modification in Table 4 and the measures in Appendix 5. Those three facts together are what
141: make it acceptable to study the product in this population.
142: 
143: High-grade serous ovarian carcinoma carries a poor long-term prognosis. Women with
144: platinum-resistant disease, residual disease after surgery, or homologous recombination
145: proficient tumours have the shortest progression-free survival.
146: 
147: Kelvaparib (KLV-3308) is an oral PARP1-selective inhibitor. By selectively inhibiting and trapping
148: poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase 1 on damaged DNA it prevents single-strand break repair, so that
149: replication forks collapse into double-strand breaks that tumours deficient in homologous
150: recombination cannot repair. Because the effect is rapid and extensive, myelosuppression is a
151: recognised risk and is mitigated by the blood count monitoring and the dose modification rules in
152:  Product: Kelvaparib (KLV-3308)

158: In the first-in-human study, the maximum tolerated dose was 300 mg orally twice daily on a
159: continuous schedule; the next higher dose exceeded it owing to myelosuppression and
160: prolonged anaemia. These findings support the dose and schedule selected for the present
161: study.
162: 
163: 1.3 Non-clinical experience
164: 
165: Non-clinical pharmacology established activity at exposures achievable in the clinic and
166: characterised the relationship between exposure and effect. Safety pharmacology found no

169: the investigator brochure; the findings were monitorable, and reversible on withdrawal at the
170: exposures tested. Genotoxicity assays were negative. The full non-clinical package, including

1. PURPOSE AND SCOPE
This guide states the house conventions that apply to every clinical document prepared
for the kelvaparib programme, including clinical study reports and their appendices,
protocols and amendments, statistical analysis plans, synopses and periodic safety
reports. It governs expression, terminology and presentation. It does not govern
document architecture, which follows ICH E3 for clinical study reports and the
applicable ICH guideline for other document types.
Where this guide and an ICH guideline both address a point, the guideline prevails and
this guide is read as supplementing it. Where a departure from this guide is deliberate,
the reason is recorded in the document review record.
2. DOCUMENT IDENTIFICATION AND VERSION CONTROL

Every page carries the product name with its development code, the document type and
the document date, in that order.

Every page carries a page number in the form "Page n of N".

The indication is stated on every page of documents that span more than one study.
3. COMPOUND, ARM AND TREATMENT NAMING

The compound is named "kelvaparib" in body text. The development code KLV-3308 is
used at first mention in a document, in page footers and on title pages, and is not
repeated in body text thereafter.

In a randomised study, arm labels state the agent and the dose, as in "Kelvaparib
300 mg". The comparator is named as it appears in the protocol, and is not
abbreviated.

In a dose-escalation study, cohorts are labelled by dose alone, as in "300 mg",
because the agent is common to every cohort.

Arm and cohort labels are identical in every table, figure, listing and narrative
within a document set. A label is not shortened to fit a column.
4. TERMINOLOGY

Adverse event terminology follows the coding dictionary in force. Verbatim terms are
not used in narrative text where a coded preferred term exists.

"Subject" is used throughout, not "patient", in clinical study reports and their
appendices. "Patient" is permitted in documents written for a non-technical
readership.

has an interest that would compromise independence. Members declare interests before
appointment and whenever an interest arises.

the charter, after any prespecified interim analysis, and at any time at the request of its chair or
the sponsor.

The committee receives disposition, exposure, adverse events by system organ class and
preferred term, serious events, deaths, laboratory data and, where the charter provides for it,
unblinded efficacy data. The statistician preparing the data reports to the committee and not to
the study team.

are discussed, and a closed session at which the committee alone reviews the data by treatment
group. Minutes of the closed session are held by the committee and released to the sponsor
only at the end of the study.

def analyze_study(name, ae_file, adsl_file, trt_col='TRT01P', kelva_val=None):
    ae = pd.read_csv(ae_file)
    adsl = pd.read_csv(adsl_file)
    print(f'=== STUDY {name} ===')
    if kelva_val is None:
        kelva_val = [x for x in adsl[trt_col].unique() if 'placebo' not in str(x).lower()]
    elif isinstance(kelva_val, str):
        kelva_val = [kelva_val]
    
    print('Total subjects:', len(adsl))
    print('Kelvaparib subjects:', len(adsl[adsl[trt_col].isin(kelva_val)]))
    
    # Merge treatment info onto AE
    ae = ae.merge(adsl[[ 'USUBJID', trt_col]], on='USUBJID', how='left')
    
    # Filter for kelvaparib
    ae_k = ae[ae[trt_col].isin(kelva_val)]
    
    for term in ['Myelodysplastic syndrome', 'Acute myeloid leukaemia', 'Pneumonitis', 'Anaemia']:
        sub_ae = ae_k[ae_k['AEDECOD'].str.lower() == term.lower()]
        n_subj = sub_ae['USUBJID'].nunique()
        n_g3plus = sub_ae[sub_ae['AETOXGR'] >= 3]['USUBJID'].nunique()
        n_sae = sub_ae[sub_ae['AESER'] == 'Y']['USUBJID'].nunique()
        n_fatal = sub_ae[sub_ae['AEOUT'] == 'FATAL']['USUBJID'].nunique() if 'AEOUT' in sub_ae.columns else 0
        if 'AESDTH' in sub_ae.columns:
            n_fatal = max(n_fatal, sub_ae[sub_ae['AESDTH'] == 'Y']['USUBJID'].nunique())
        print(f'  {term}: n_subj={n_subj}, g3+={n_g3plus}, sae={n_sae}, fatal={n_fatal}')

12.6 Safety conclusions

The safety profile observed was consistent with that anticipated for oral PARP1-selective inhibitor in this population. The events that

13 DISCUSSION AND OVERALL CONCLUSIONS

Study KLV-7701 evaluated kelvaparib in recurrent ovarian carcinoma after prior platinum-based therapy, platinum-sensitive or
platinum-resistant. Kelvaparib prolonged progression-free survival compared with placebo in recurrent ovarian carcinoma after prior
platinum-based therapy, platinum-sensitive or platinum-resistant (stratified hazard ratio 0.64, 95 per cent CI 0.50 to 0.81; stratified
log-rank p = 0.0002), and the primary endpoint was met. The objective response rate (54.5 per cent) was also significantly higher with
kelvaparib (Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel p < 0.0001); overall survival, the next endpoint in the testing hierarchy, did not differ (stratified
log-rank p = 0.8651), and findings below that point are descriptive. The safety profile was dominated by anaemia and myelosuppression,
both on-target consequences of the mechanism of action. Myelodysplastic syndrome or acute myeloid leukaemia occurred in 1.4 per cent
of subjects (Section 12.2.6). Limitations should be borne in mind. The study was open-label, which may influence investigator
assessment of response and reporting of subjective adverse events. Follow-up was ongoing at the data cut-off and time-to-event
estimates are therefore immature. Taken together, the results of study KLV-7701 support the continued development of kelvaparib at 300
mg, with weekly blood counts for the first month and monthly thereafter, in high-grade serous ovarian carcinoma.

The population enrolled was consistent with the intended population and with the eligibility criteria. Exposure was sufficient to
characterise both the efficacy and the safety of the regimen. The primary analysis was performed as planned; the sensitivity analyses the
statistical analysis plan lists are not reported here.

The population enrolled was the population the protocol described. Median age, performance status and prior therapy were consistent
with the eligibility criteria, and there is no indication that the study enrolled a population easier to treat than the one intended.

Exposure was adequate. The median relative dose intensity indicates that the regimen as written could be delivered, and the pattern of
reduction and interruption was consistent with the toxicities anticipated for oral PARP1-selective inhibitor.

The efficacy result should be read together with its confidence interval and with the maturity of the follow-up. Because the study was
randomised, the comparison is internally controlled and the estimate does not depend on an external assumption about how this
population would otherwise have fared.

The safety profile was consistent with the mechanism and with the earlier clinical experience. The events reported most often, and those
most often reaching grade 3 or higher, were those for which the protocol required specific monitoring, which indicates that the monitoring
was directed at the right things.

96 subjects (15.3 per cent) discontinued study treatment because of an adverse event. That figure, rather than the overall incidence of
events, is the measure of whether the regimen is tolerable in practice, because it counts the events that could not be managed by dose
modification.

Deaths were reviewed individually. Those attributed to an adverse event are described in the narratives; the remainder are recorded as
disease outcomes and are consistent with what would be expected in this population over this period.

The limitations of this study should be borne in mind. Follow-up at this analysis is limited and the longer time-to-event estimates are
immature. The study was open-label, so investigator assessment of any subjective endpoint may have been influenced by knowledge of
